blocks.prompt: The Plate That Tells You What to Eat
blocks.text: Long ago the food guide was a pyramid. It was a triangle with bread at the bottom. Lots of people looked at it and did not know what to do with it. So in 2011 the guide changed into a plate. A plate makes more sense, because you eat off a plate. The new guide is called MyPlate. It has four parts: fruits, vegetables, grains, and protein. A little circle beside it stands for milk or yogurt. The most important part is easy to remember. Half your plate should be fruits and vegetables.

3.title: The Plate That Tells You What to Eat

meta.templateLabel: The Plate That Tells You What to Eat

blocks.prompt: Why a Plate and Not a Pyramid
blocks.text: For almost twenty years, American kids learned about food from a pyramid. It was printed on cereal boxes and taped to classroom walls. Bread and rice sat in a wide band at the bottom. Sweets sat in a tiny point at the top. The idea was simple, but the picture was not. People stared at the pyramid and could not tell how much of anything to actually eat. In 2011 the government tried something new. They drew a plate. Nobody eats from a pyramid, but everybody eats from a plate, so the new guide showed food the way you really see it. MyPlate has four sections. Fruits and vegetables together fill one half. Grains and protein foods fill the other half. A small circle sits off to the side for milk or yogurt. The plate does not tell you exactly what to cook. It tells you what your meal should look like when you glance down at it. That is the whole trick. A good food guide has to work in the two seconds before you pick up your fork.

4.title: The Plate That Tells You What to Eat
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Plate That Tells You What to Eat

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Starch is a long chain of sugar
Whole grains keep the bran and the germ
Protein breaks down into amino acids
Fiber feeds the bacteria in your gut
You build more bone than you lose until your mid twenties

blocks.prompt: Every Section Does a Different Job
blocks.text: A food guide only looks like a picture of lunch. Underneath, it is a picture of jobs. Grains are mostly starch, and starch is a long chain of sugar. Your body snaps the chain apart and burns the pieces for fuel. Whole grains keep the bran and the germ, the outer coat and the seed's living core, so they carry fiber and minerals that white flour has lost. That is why the guide says to make half your grains whole. Protein foods, like beans, fish, eggs, and chicken, break down into amino acids. Your body reuses those pieces to build muscle, skin, and the enzymes that run your digestion. You cannot store amino acids the way you store fat, so you need some most days. Fruits and vegetables get half the plate for a reason that is not about calories at all. They carry vitamin C, potassium, folate, and fiber, and they carry them with very few calories. Fiber is the strangest part. You cannot digest it. It travels all the way to your large intestine and feeds the trillions of bacteria living there. Dairy sits in the side circle for calcium. Your skeleton is not a finished object. It is torn down and rebuilt constantly, and until about your mid twenties you are building more bone than you lose. Calcium is the raw material for that work, and the window closes. Nothing on the plate is a treat or a punishment. Each section is a delivery van, and each one carries something your body cannot make on its own.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: First US food guide: 1916
The Basic Seven wheel: 1943, during the war
The pyramid was invented in Sweden in 1974
The US pyramid: 1992. MyPyramid: 2005
MyPlate: 2011
Harvard published a rival plate the same year

blocks.prompt: A Hundred Years of Telling People What to Eat
blocks.text: Governments have been drawing pictures of dinner for over a century, and every picture tells you as much about its moment as it does about nutrition. The United States published its first food guide in 1916, written for children. In 1943, with the country at war and food rationed, the Department of Agriculture released the Basic Seven, a wheel with seven wedges. It was thorough and almost useless. Nobody could hold seven categories in mind while standing in a grocery store. In 1956 it was cut down to the Basic Four, which lasted more than twenty years. The pyramid came from Sweden. In 1974, food prices were climbing, and a Swedish cooperative wanted a chart showing which foods were both cheap and necessary. The answer they drew was a triangle: staples at the wide base, luxuries at the narrow tip. The shape was so intuitive that it spread across Europe, and the United States adopted its own version in 1992. The American pyramid ran into trouble immediately. The food industry fought over which foods sat near the shameful point at the top. Meat and dairy groups objected to being ranked above bread. The chart that finally shipped was a compromise, and a compromise is a hard thing to read. When the government revised it in 2005 into MyPyramid, the categories became colored stripes with no words on them at all, and a tiny figure climbing stairs up the side. It was clean, modern, and unreadable. MyPlate arrived in 2011 and admitted something the earlier charts had ignored. People do not think in servings or wedges or stripes. They think in meals. So the guide became a plate with four sections, half of it fruits and vegetables, and a cup on the side. You can check yourself against it in one glance, without counting anything. Not everyone was satisfied. That same year, nutrition researchers at Harvard published a rival plate. Theirs replaced the milk cup with water, added a bottle of healthy oil, insisted that the grains be whole rather than half, and told readers to stay active. Their argument was that the government's plate was shaped partly by the industries the government also promotes, and that a food guide should say what the evidence says. Both plates agree on the loud part: fill half of it with plants. The argument is over the quiet parts, and the argument is not finished.

6.title: The Plate That Tells You What to Eat
6.subtitle: A reading and analysis sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Plate That Tells You What to Eat

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A triangle ranks. A plate only divides
Swedish cooperative, 1974: cheap plus essential
US pyramid 1992: negotiated with industry
MyPlate 2011: proportions, not hierarchy
Harvard's rival plate: water, oils, whole grains
Both plates fill half with plants

blocks.prompt: The Shape of an Argument
blocks.text: Look at a food guide long enough and you notice it is not really a chart. It is an argument compressed into a shape. Consider what a plate has to do. It must summarize a field where the evidence is genuinely messy, survive being reprinted on a classroom poster, be understood in under two seconds by a tired person holding a fork, and pass review by an agency whose other job is supporting American farmers. Any picture that satisfies all four is going to be a compromise, and the interesting question is which parts got compromised. Start with the shape itself. The pyramid was invented in Sweden in 1974, when food prices were rising and a consumer cooperative wanted to show which foods were both cheap and essential. A triangle answers that question elegantly. The wide base is what you live on, the narrow tip is what you can skip. But a triangle is an abstraction, and it ranks. It implies a hierarchy of virtue, with bread as good and fat as sin, and it never tells you what to put on your actual plate at six o'clock. When the United States adapted the pyramid in 1992, that ranking became a battlefield. Meat and dairy producers objected to sitting near the disgraced tip. The chart that finally shipped had been negotiated. MyPlate, in 2011, gave up on ranking altogether. A plate does not stack anything. It divides, and division is a much weaker claim than hierarchy. It says only that a meal should have roughly these proportions. That weakness is precisely why it works, because the message survives being glanced at. But look at what the plate still cannot say. It shows a section labeled protein, and a fillet of salmon and a hot dog both qualify. It shows grains, and a bowl of oats and a slice of white bread both qualify, with a footnote asking you to make half of them whole. It gives dairy its own permanent seat beside the plate, alone among foods. Critics noticed that the Department of Agriculture writes the guide and also runs marketing programs for dairy and beef, and that no chart is neutral when its author has two jobs. That is why, months after MyPlate launched, nutrition researchers at Harvard published a competing plate. It looks similar and disagrees in nearly every detail that matters. Water replaces milk. Oils get their own bottle. Grains must be whole, not half. Red meat is pushed to the edge with a warning. A small running figure appears in the corner, because exercise is not food but the researchers wanted it on the picture anyway. Notice that the two plates do not disagree about the loudest instruction. Both fill half with vegetables and fruit. That part is not controversial, because it rests on some of the sturdiest evidence in nutrition. Across decades and across countries, people who eat more plants have less heart disease. The fights are over the quieter half of the picture, where the evidence thins out and the interests thicken. So a food guide is a shape that has to hold all of this at once: a science still arguing with itself, an industry that would like a favorable slice, and a person who has two seconds and is already hungry. It will always be too simple. It has to be. The honest way to read one is not as a fact but as a claim, and to ask, of every line drawn, who wanted it there.
